title: Predict how by-value parameters and ref, out, or in affect caller storage

rubric.point: `item` receives a copy of the reference in `first`, initially referring to the same object.
`item.Count = 7` mutates that shared object, so the change is visible through `first`.
Assigning a new object to `item` changes only the by-value parameter; `first` still refers to the original object.
`replacement` aliases `second`, so assigning `item` to it makes `second` refer to the new object whose count is 12.

questions.model:
`item` holds a copy of `first`'s reference. Both initially refer to the original box, so changing `item.Count` changes the object seen through `first` to `7`.

Reassigning `item` stores a new reference only in the local parameter. It leaves `first` pointing to the original box. `replacement`, however, aliases the caller's `second` variable. Assigning `item` to `replacement` therefore replaces the reference stored in `second`. The caller finishes with two different objects: `first.Count` is `7`, and `second.Count` is `12`.

rubric.point: `out` permits an uninitialized caller variable because the method is responsible for assigning the output.
`reserved` aliases `count`, so the assignment stores 0 in `count`; returning false does not undo or suppress that assignment.
Every normal return path must assign an `out` parameter; deleting the assignment leaves the false-return path unassigned.

questions.model:
`out` allows `count` to be uninitialized at the call because the method must produce its value. `reserved` aliases `count`, so `reserved = 0` writes directly into the caller's variable. The Boolean return value reports failure separately and does not cancel that write.

Deleting the assignment would leave a normal return path that does not assign `reserved`. C# rejects that method because an `out` parameter must be assigned before every normal return.

rubric.point: `in` provides readonly access to the storage holding the caller's reference.
`Clear()` mutates the referenced list without replacing that reference, so the caller observes the mutation.
Assigning a new list would write through the readonly parameter, which `in` forbids; readonly passing does not make the referenced object immutable.

questions.model:
`in` gives the method a readonly alias to the caller's variable holding the list reference. It prevents writing a replacement reference through `items`.

`Clear()` changes the existing list object without reassigning the reference. The caller refers to that same object and therefore sees an empty list. `items = new List<int>();` would assign through the readonly alias, so it is rejected. The readonly parameter does not make the list itself immutable.
